newsitem.title: UK: EMU leeway should be used sparingly - Lamfalussy.
newsitem.headline: EMU leeway should be used sparingly - Lamfalussy.

text.p: The rules for qualifying for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) allow some deviation from the set targets but such leeway should be used sparingly, the head of the European Union's future central bank said on Monday.

Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute -- the forerunner of the European Central Bank (ECB) -- said the key to interpreting the Masstricht Treaty's economic targets was "sustainability".
"In essence, we should stick to both the spirit and the letter of the Treaty," Lamfalussy said in a speech at the London School of Economics.
Governments must bring their budget deficits down to three percent of output and outstanding government debt to 60 percent of output in 1997 if they wish to join monetary union.
While the Maastricht treaty established these two "reference values" which should not be exceeded, it accepts deviations from them on certain conditions, Lamfalussy, a Belgian, said.
There has been a growing debate in recent weeks in financial markets and political circles as to whether or not a single currency will be launched as planned on January 1, 1999.
The debate has focused on concerns that Germany, Europe's locomotive for growth and by far the biggest economy, would itself not satisfy the letter of Maastricht's rules this year.
"Deviations from the reference values should be granted sparingly by interpreting the words used by the Treaty in a carefully restrictive way," he said.
"Compliance with the reference values should be regarded as sufficient for eligibility only if the deficit and debt ratios observed for 1997 are genuinely sustainable."
"In short, in case of doubt when applying the second and third prescriptions of the treaty, we should lean towards caution," he told the conference.

Earlier on Monday Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, a member of Germany's powerful Bundesbank, said he doubted the German government would reach its goal of cutting its budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
He also noted that there was room for interpretation of the Treaty but said liberal interpretation should not risk stability.

"The Maastricht Treaty allows a certain leeway at least with regard to the fiscal criteria. Such an attempt to start monetary union at all costs must be clearly rejected because of the risks to stability this would entail," Kuehbacher said.

The HWWA institute, one of six independent bodies whose estimates are used by Bonn, also expressed doubts about Germany's ability to hit the Maastricht targets, but also raised the question of a delay to monetary union.
"Under strict interpretation, only a few countries will fulfil the entry criteria, so that a delay of the start of EMU would be conceivable," HWWA said.
The Institute said without a stronger economic turnaround Germany itself was a risk of missing the key total public sector deficit target of three percent.
The EMU delay debate intensified over the weekend when an independent economic adviser to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl predicted a delay of up to one year in the EMU project.
Herbert Hax, head of the influential "five wise men" government advisory panel, said Bonn in all likelihood would not satisfy the debt and deficit targets laid out in Maastricht this year.
"If you take the stability criteria seriously, Germany will probably not be able to introduce the euro as planned in 1999," Hax said in a weekend German newspaper.
